findings.heading: Substituir valores/hierarquia (Overwrite values/hierarchy)
findings.proposition: The prose claims that after the chunk runs, a person who ever answered affirmatively shows only that single affirmative value in symptoms_ever; the Portuguese chunk tests str_detect(.x, "Sim") while the data values are "Yes"/"No", so no row can ever become "Sim" and a rolled value such as "No; Yes; Yes" is rewritten to "No" by the second branch.
findings.reader_consequence: A Portuguese reader running the chunk sees the opposite of what the text promises: people who did report symptoms are labelled "No". Anyone copying this hierarchy pattern into real cleaning code silently inverts a Yes/No/Unknown priority rule.

findings.heading: Subdividão com grupos (Slice with groups)
findings.proposition: The DANGER note states Mariah has two encounters on her latest date, 6 January, and that with_ties = FALSE keeps the earlier of the two; in the Portuguese data chunk her dates parse as 2020-05-01, 2020-01-06 and 2020-01-06, so her latest date is 1 May 2020 with a single encounter and there is no tie at all.
findings.reader_consequence: The reader looks for the tie that the warning describes, does not find it in the printed table, and cannot see the failure mode the section exists to teach. The whole motivation for the tie-breaking example that follows is lost.

findings.heading: Subdividão com grupos (Slice with groups)
findings.proposition: The prose states that the slice kept only Amrish's 5 January row and only Brian's 7 January row; with the Portuguese date strings the same chunk keeps Amrish's 2020-05-01 row and Brian's 2020-05-01 row, because the reformatted dates ("01/05/2020", "01/02/2020") are parsed by format = "%d/%m/%Y" as 1 May and 1 February.
findings.reader_consequence: The dates the text names do not appear in the table beside it, so the reader cannot confirm what slice_max() did and may conclude they ran the code wrongly. The corrupted example dataset also silently changes every later date-based result in the chapter.

findings.heading: Subdividão com grupos (Slice with groups)
findings.proposition: The prose states that after the two-step slice the row kept for Mariah on 6 January is encounter 3 at 08:32 rather than encounter 2 at 07:25; with the Portuguese data the second slice_max() on time changes nothing and the row kept for Mariah is encounter 1 on 2020-05-01 at 12:00.
findings.reader_consequence: The reader cannot verify that the second slice_max() broke a tie, because in the Portuguese output no tie was broken. The technique the section teaches appears to have no effect.

findings.heading: Usando o R base (Using base R)
findings.proposition: The translation gives the command for returning unique rows as df[!duplicado(df),]; duplicado() is not an R function, and every other sentence in the same segment names duplicated().
findings.reader_consequence: A reader who copies the line gets 'could not find function "duplicado"' and has no way to tell from the text whether the base R idiom or their own typing is at fault.
